title: Permission denied on a file you can read
tagline: The service cannot read its own configuration. ls -l says the permissions are correct. Two different mechanisms say no.
environment: Service restored from a backup archive
symptoms: Service fails at startup with 'cannot open /etc/myapp/app.conf: Permission denied'
ls -l shows root:svcapp with mode 640 — svcapp should be able to read it
The same config worked before a restore from backup
Running the binary by hand as root works
objectives: Separate classic Unix permissions from SELinux labelling and ACLs
Read ls -Z and identify a wrong context
Choose the correct relabel/restore command instead of disabling a security control
framework: Who is the process, and which user/group does it run as?
What do the mode bits allow for that identity?
What do the extended controls (ACLs, SELinux labels) allow?

evidence.label: The exact error and identity
evidence.command: systemctl status myapp --no-pager | tail -3; systemctl show -p User,Group myapp
evidence.output:
Nov 17 10:02:11 host myapp[4242]: FATAL: cannot open /etc/myapp/app.conf: Permission denied
User=svcapp
Group=svcapp
evidence.insight: The process runs as svcapp. EACCES is returned by the kernel, not by the application's own logic.

evidence.label: Classic permissions
evidence.output:
-rw-r----- 1 root svcapp 512 Nov 17 09:58 /etc/myapp/app.conf

f: /etc/myapp/app.conf
drwxr-xr-x root root /
drwxr-xr-x root root etc
drwxr-x--- root svcapp myapp
drwxr-xr-x root root /
-rw-r----- root svcapp app.conf
evidence.insight: owner root (rw), group svcapp (r), others none. svcapp is in the group, so mode bits allow a read, and every parent directory is traversable. Unix permissions are not the blocker.

evidence.label: Extended controls
evidence.output:
unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 /etc/myapp/app.conf

# file: etc/myapp/app.conf
# owner: root
# group: svcapp
user::rw-
group::r--
other::---
evidence.insight: The SELinux type is user_home_t, not the type the service is allowed to read (etc_t). The tar restore preserved the archive's labels. No ACLs are involved.

evidence.label: Confirm SELinux is the denial
evidence.output:
type=AVC msg=audit(1763380931.442:812): avc:  denied  { read } for  pid=4242 comm="java" name="app.conf" dev="dm-0" ino=131 addr=?
  scontext=system_u:system_r:myapp_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 tclass=file permissive=0
evidence.insight: An explicit AVC denial: myapp_t tried to read a user_home_t file. That is the kernel refusing, and it names both contexts so there is nothing to infer.

evidence.label: What the label should be
evidence.output:
/etc/myapp(/.*)?   system_u:object_r:myapp_etc_t:s0

/etc/myapp/app.conf has context unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0
should be system_u:object_r:myapp_etc_t:s0
evidence.insight: The policy has a rule for this path. matchpathcon reports the mismatch directly: the file's label should be myapp_etc_t.

evidence.label: Why the restore caused it
evidence.output:
-rw-r----- root/svcapp  512 2026-11-16 22:10 ./etc/myapp/app.conf
(no SELinux xattrs preserved; archive created without --selinux)
evidence.insight: The archive was created without --selinux, so extraction wrote files with default (home) labels. The permissions were preserved but the security context was not.

hypotheses.text: The file's mode bits deny svcapp read access.
hypotheses.why: Mode 640 with group svcapp and svcapp as the process group allows a read; every parent directory is traversable.

hypotheses.text: SELinux denies the read because the restored file carries the wrong type.
hypotheses.why: An AVC denial names myapp_t reading user_home_t, and matchpathcon says the label should be myapp_etc_t.
getfacl shows only the base entries, no extended ACLs.

hypotheses.text: The service is running as the wrong user.
hypotheses.why: It runs as svcapp, which is the file's group owner.

solution.root_cause: The backup archive was created and extracted without preserving SELinux extended attributes, so /etc/myapp/app.conf was written with the default user_home_t type instead of myapp_etc_t. Unix permissions are correct, but SELinux applies in addition to them, and the policy has no allowance for myapp_t reading user_home_t.
solution.resolution: Relabel the path to what policy expects: restorecon -Rv /etc/myapp (or semanage fcontext -a -t myapp_etc_t '/etc/myapp(/.*)?' followed by restorecon if a custom path was never labelled). For future restores, create archives with tar --selinux and extract as root so the labels are preserved.
solution.verification: ls -Z shows myapp_etc_t; matchpathcon -V reports no mismatch; the service starts and stays up; ausearch -m avc -ts recent shows no new denials for the unit. Confirm with systemctl restart and a log line proving the config was read.
lessons: Permission denied can come from mode bits, ACLs or SELinux. Check them in that order, and read the AVC rather than guessing.
SELinux is a second lock, not a replacement for the first. Correct mode bits plus a wrong label still fails.
Backups that omit extended attributes are not faithful backups. Test restores, not just backups.

resolution_options.why: Applies the policy's expected label to the path and everything under it.

resolution_options.text: Add a permanent fcontext rule for the path, then relabel
resolution_options.why: Correct when the path is custom and has no existing policy rule.
Changes nothing relevant: the blocker is the label, and it also weakens access for others.
Removes a security control to hide a labelling error.
Does not fix the label and violates least privilege.

interview_questions.q: A process gets Permission denied but the mode bits look correct. What else can deny access?
interview_questions.a: An ACL, an SELinux denial, an immutable attribute, a read-only filesystem, or a parent directory issue. The AVC audit record and getfacl tell you which, and namei -l checks the whole path.

interview_questions.q: How does SELinux decide whether to allow an access?
interview_questions.a: It compares the source context (the process, e.g. myapp_t) with the target context (the file, e.g. myapp_etc_t) against the loaded policy. If no rule allows the access, it denies and logs an AVC.

interview_questions.q: What is the correct way to give a custom path a persistent label?
interview_questions.a: semanage fcontext -a -t <type> '<regex>', then restorecon -R on the path so existing files are relabelled to match the rule.
